title: Solve Equations by Graphing: Find the x-Intercepts
description: Start with an equation that's painful by hand, then build Zero, Graph, Click step by step until you can solve it in Desmos, and use it on any one-variable equation.

blocks.html:
Try this one first

Solve for \(x\):

\[\sqrt{x-4}+\sqrt{x+1}=5\]

Give it an honest 30 seconds on paper. No calculator yet.

You don't have to finish. Just decide how you'd start, and how long it would take.

content.prompt: Most students start by squaring both sides. Squared correctly, what does the left side \(\sqrt{x-4}+\sqrt{x+1}\) become?
content.hint: Squaring a sum is \((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\). What are \(a\) and \(b\) here, and what is \(a^2\) when \(a\) is a square root?
content.solution:
Let \(a=\sqrt{x-4}\) and \(b=\sqrt{x+1}\).
\((a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2\), and squaring a square root undoes it: \(a^2=x-4\), \(b^2=x+1\).
The middle term is \(2\sqrt{x-4}\sqrt{x+1}=2\sqrt{(x-4)(x+1)}\).
So the answer is choice B.
content.explanation: That's the honest version, and look what's still in the middle: a square root. By hand you'd isolate it, square again, solve, then test every answer for extraneous solutions. Four steps, a trap in each. Desmos does this one in about 20 seconds, and by the end of this lesson you will too.

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.
figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

blocks.html:
Spot the situation

The move: Zero, Graph, Click.

Why it pays: Desmos doesn't care what kind of equation it is, and it shows you every solution.

One caution: Desmos gives decimals. Exact answer choices? Type them in and compare.

What made that equation a graphing problem?

  • One equation
  • One variable
  • The question wants its solutions (or how many there are)

Key idea: That's the whole checklist. The algebra doesn't have to be ugly. Unless you can do it in your head, like \(3x=12\), graphing is usually faster and more accurate.

content.prompt: Which equation is faster to solve in your head than in Desmos?
content.hint: Look for the one you could answer before Desmos even finished loading.
content.explanation: Yes: one mental step gives \(x=5\). The other three are one equation in one variable with more than a step of algebra, so graph them. Even the linear one with fractions: clearing denominators is where signs get dropped.

blocks.html:
Start with the simplest case

This equation already has zero on one side:

\[x^2-5x+6=0\]

The graph of \(x^2-5x+6\) is open. Click the two places where the curve meets the horizontal axis (the x-axis). Desmos labels each point.

calculator.title: Click where it meets the axis

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.
figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

content.prompt: Which labeled points did you find where the graph meets the x-axis?
content.hint: Click the graph exactly where it crosses the horizontal axis and read each full label.
content.explanation: Right: \((2,0)\) and \((3,0)\). Both have height \(0\), which is the whole point of the next screen.

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.

blocks.html:
Why those points are solutions

Every point on the x-axis has height \(0\). So at \((2,0)\) and \((3,0)\), the expression \(x^2-5x+6\) equals \(0\).

A point where a graph meets the x-axis is an x-intercept. Its first number, the x-coordinate, is a solution.

Key idea: Every x-intercept is a solution. Here, \(x=2\) and \(x=3\).

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.
figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

content.prompt: The graph of an expression has x-intercepts at \((-1,0)\) and \((4,0)\). Which equation do \(x=-1\) and \(x=4\) both solve?
content.hint: What is the height of every point on the x-axis?
content.explanation: Yes. At an x-intercept the height is \(0\), so each x-coordinate makes the expression equal zero.

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.
figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

blocks.html:
Step up: make the zero yourself

Most equations don't come with a zero. Take \(x^2+1=4x\). An x-intercept only shows where something equals \(0\), so make one: subtract \(4x\) from both sides.

\[x^2-4x+1=0\]

The graph of \(x^2-4x+1\) is open. Click both x-intercepts: about \(0.268\) and \(3.732\). Those two decimals solve the original \(x^2+1=4x\). No factoring, no quadratic formula.

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.
figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

content.title: Make the zero, then graph
content.instructions_html: Rewrite \(2x^2+5=7x\) with zero on one side, then enter the expression to graph. A bare expression works; \(y=\) is optional.

feedback.success_message_html: That's it. Click both x-intercepts: \(x=1\) and \(x=2.5\) solve \(2x^2+5=7x\).
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Enter only the expression (no equals sign), with everything moved to one side.

attempt_based_hints.message_html: Which term on the right needs to move so that side becomes \(0\)?
Subtract \(7x\) from both sides. Keep the \(2x^2\) and the \(+5\).

blocks.html:
It works on any shape

Nothing about Zero, Graph, Click needs a quadratic. Try a square root: \(\sqrt{x-1}=2\).

Zero: subtract \(2\), so you graph \(\sqrt{x-1}-2\).

Desmos tip: type sqrt and Desmos draws the radical. Press the right arrow to step out of it before you type the rest.

figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

content.title: Graph a square root
content.instructions_html: Enter the expression to graph for \(\sqrt{x-1}=2\), then click its x-intercept.

feedback.success_message_html: Nice. The intercept is \((5,0)\), so \(x=5\). Notice the graph starts at \(x=1\): Desmos only draws where the square root exists.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Enter only the expression (no equals sign), with everything moved to one side.

attempt_based_hints.message_html: Subtract \(2\) from both sides, so the right side is \(0\).
Type sqrt, then x-1, press the right arrow, then type -2.

figure.alt: The goal problem: the square root of x minus 4, plus the square root of x plus 1, equals 5.
figure.caption: Keep this in view. Every step here builds toward it.

content.prompt: The graph of \(\left|x-3\right|-2\) is open. What are all the solutions to \(\left|x-3\right|=2\)?
content.hint: Click every place the V-shaped graph meets the x-axis. There may be more than one.
content.explanation: Both: the V meets the axis at \((1,0)\) and \((5,0)\). By hand, the left one is the solution people forget. The graph doesn't let you.

content.instructions_html:
You have every tool you need. Solve \(\sqrt{x-4}+\sqrt{x+1}=5\).

Zero first, then enter the expression to graph.

feedback.success_message_html: That's the graph. Click where it meets the x-axis before you continue.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Enter only the expression (no equals sign), with everything moved to one side.

attempt_based_hints.message_html: Zero first: which number can you move so one side becomes \(0\)?
Subtract \(5\) from both sides. Then type sqrt for each radical, pressing the right arrow to step out before typing +.

content.prompt: Click the x-intercept. What is the solution to \(\sqrt{x-4}+\sqrt{x+1}=5\)?
content.hint: Click the one place the graph meets the x-axis and read the first number in its label.
content.solution:
Subtract 5 to get zero on one side and graph \(\sqrt{x-4}+\sqrt{x+1}-5\).
The graph starts at \(x=4\) and crosses the x-axis once, at \((8,0)\).
So the solution is \(x=8\).
content.explanation: \(x=8\). Check it: \(\sqrt{4}+\sqrt{9}=2+3=5\). One intercept, one solution, and no extraneous answers to weed out, because you never squared anything. That's the problem you didn't want to touch ten minutes ago.

Same three moves, every equation. The card beside this text is the version to remember.

Then report: answer what the question actually asks. The right letter, the right form, the right one of several solutions.

choices: Solve by hand. It's linear, so Desmos won't help.
Graph both sides and read the y-intercept.
content.hint: Which plan does the Zero step before graphing?
content.explanation: Zero first, then graph: the intercept is at \(x=5.4\). Graphing the left side alone finds where it equals \(0\), not \(4\). And linear doesn't mean by hand: clearing those fractions takes three steps, each a chance to drop a sign.

blocks.html:
Variation: decimals vs. exact choices

The graph of \(x^2-7\) crosses near \(-2.646\) and \(2.646\). SAT choices are often exact, like radicals or fractions.

Don't eyeball it. Type each choice into Desmos and compare decimals.

Try it: on new rows, type \(\sqrt{7}\), \(\frac{\sqrt{14}}{2}\), and \(\frac{7}{2}\). Which one is about \(2.646\)?

figure.alt: Recap card. 1, Zero: move everything to one side. 2, Graph: type what's left into Desmos; swap any other letter for x. 3, Click: every x-intercept is a solution; count them all, touches too. Caution: exact choices and a decimal graph, type the choices in and compare.
figure.caption: Zero, Graph, Click.

content.prompt: The intercepts are about \(-2.646\) and \(2.646\). Which exact answer matches?
content.hint: Which value did Desmos show as about \(2.646\)? Then check how many intercepts the graph has.
content.solution:
Type each exact choice into Desmos: \(\sqrt{7}\approx2.646\), \(\frac{\sqrt{14}}{2}\approx1.871\), \(\frac{7}{2}=3.5\).
Only \(\sqrt{7}\) matches.
The graph has a negative and a positive intercept, so include both signs.
So the answer is choice A.
content.explanation: \(\sqrt{7}\approx2.646\), and the graph has an intercept on each side, so \(x=\pm\sqrt{7}\).

figure.caption: Zero, Graph, Click.

blocks.html:
Variation: how many solutions?

Each distinct x-intercept is one solution. A graph that only touches the axis and turns around still counts.

Three graphs are loaded but hidden. Click the colored circle beside a row to show it (the picture shows where). Show one at a time and count its intercepts:

  1. \(x^2-5x+6\)
  2. \((x-3)^2\)
  3. \(x^2+4\)

figure.caption: Click the circle to show or hide a graph.

content.prompt: Match each equation to its number of distinct real solutions.
choices: All three have two, because all three contain \(x^2\).
content.hint: Count crossings and touches. A touch gives one x-value.
content.explanation: Two, one, none. The middle graph touches at \((3,0)\) and turns back: that's one solution, not zero.

Variation: the empty-looking graph

For \(x^2+320=36x\), the graph of \(x^2-36x+320\) is open. It looks like there's nothing there.

Before you say "no solution": zoom out. Use the minus button or scroll until you find the curve.

figure.alt: Recap card. 1, Zero: move everything to one side. 2, Graph: type what's left into Desmos; swap any other letter for x. 3, Click: every x-intercept is a solution; count them all, touches too. Caution: exact choices and a decimal graph, type the choices in and compare.

content.prompt: After zooming out, how many real solutions does \(x^2+320=36x\) have?
content.hint: Zoom out until you can see the whole U shape, then count where it meets the x-axis.
content.solution:
Zero: \(x^2-36x+320=0\). Graph \(x^2-36x+320\).
The curve sits far to the right of the starting window. Zoomed out, it crosses the x-axis at \((16,0)\) and \((20,0)\).
So there are 2 real solutions.
content.explanation: Two, at \(x=16\) and \(x=20\). The SAT likes this one: an empty window isn't evidence of no solution.

blocks.html:
Your turn: three shapes

Three equations, three different shapes. Each gets a little less help.

  1. Absolute value. The setup screen checks your graph.
  2. A fraction, with a different letter. The setup screen checks your graph.
  3. A cubic. Just you and the calculator.

content.title: Practice 1: absolute value
content.instructions_html: Solve \(\left|2x-3\right|=x+1\). Get zero on one side, then enter the expression to graph.

feedback.success_message_html: Good. Click every x-intercept before you continue.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Enter only the expression (no equals sign), with everything moved to one side.

attempt_based_hints.message_html: Move the whole right side, \(x+1\), to the left. Both terms.
Type | for the absolute value bars and press the right arrow to step out before typing -x-1.

content.prompt: What is the sum of the solutions to \(\left|2x-3\right|=x+1\)?
content.hint: Click both intercepts. One isn't a whole number, so add its decimal.
content.solution:
Graph \(\left|2x-3\right|-x-1\) and click both x-intercepts.
Desmos labels \((0.667,0)\) and \((4,0)\).
The sum is \(0.667+4\approx4.667\), which is \(\frac{14}{3}\).
content.explanation: \(\frac{2}{3}+4=\frac{14}{3}\approx4.667\). By hand, the \(\frac{2}{3}\) comes from the negative case, the one people skip. The graph showed it to you.

content.title: Practice 2: a fraction and a new letter
content.instructions_html: Solve \(\frac{6}{t}=t-1\). Swap \(t\) for \(x\), get zero on one side, then enter the expression to graph. No need to clear the fraction.

feedback.success_message_html: Good. Click every x-intercept. The graph breaks at \(x=0\); that gap is not a crossing.
feedback.retry_message_html: Not yet. Enter only the expression (no equals sign), with everything moved to one side.

attempt_based_hints.message_html: Swap \(t\) for \(x\), then move the whole right side, \(x-1\), to the left.
Type 6/x and Desmos builds the fraction. Press the right arrow to step out before typing -x+1.

content.prompt: What is the negative solution to \(\frac{6}{t}=t-1\)?
content.hint: Click both intercepts. Which one is left of the y-axis? Report it as a value of \(t\).
content.solution:
Swap \(t\) for \(x\) and graph \(\frac{6}{x}-x+1\).
The graph meets the x-axis at \((-2,0)\) and \((3,0)\).
The negative one is \(t=-2\).

blocks.html:
Practice 3: on your own

\[x^3=4x+1\]

No setup screen this time. Use the calculator: Zero, Graph, Click. Count every intercept, and zoom out once to be sure there aren't more.

content.prompt: How many real solutions does \(x^3=4x+1\) have?
content.hint: Look closely near the y-axis as well as at the ends of the curve.
content.solution:
Zero: \(x^3-4x-1=0\). Graph \(x^3-4x-1\).
The curve crosses the x-axis near \(-1.861\), \(-0.254\), and \(2.115\).
So there are 3 real solutions.
content.explanation: Three, near \(-1.861\), \(-0.254\), and \(2.115\). This cubic doesn't factor, so there's no clean algebra route at all. The graph doesn't care.

content.prompt: What is the solution to the equation \(\sqrt{2x+7}=x-4\)?
content.hint: Zero, Graph, Click, and report only what the graph shows.
content.explanation: \(x=9\). The graph of \(\sqrt{2x+7}-x+4\) meets the axis once, at \((9,0)\). The SAT's trap is \(x=1\): squaring both sides produces it, but \(\sqrt{9}=3\) while \(1-4=-3\). The graph never shows it.

content.html:
Zero, Graph, Click

Any shape, any letter: zero on one side, graph what's left, and every intercept is a solution.
